title: Schanuel's lemma
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-module. Let $0\to K\xrightarrow{c_1}P_1\xrightarrow{p_1}M\to0$ and $0\to L\xrightarrow{c_2}P_2\xrightarrow{p_2}M\to0$ be short exact sequences [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence] of $R$-modules with $P_1$ and $P_2$ projective [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. Then there is an isomorphism of $R$-modules $K\oplus P_2\cong L\oplus P_1$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00O3 (lemma-Schanuel, line 26485), first statement. Tag verified in tags/tags: 00O3,algebra-lemma-Schanuel

proof.text: Put $N=\{(u,v)\in P_1\oplus P_2:p_1(u)+p_2(v)=0\}$, the kernel of the sum map $P_1\oplus P_2\to M$. The coordinate projections $q_1:N\to P_1$ and $q_2:N\to P_2$ are surjective: for a given $u\in P_1$, choose $v$ with $p_2(v)=-p_1(u)$, and for a given $v\in P_2$, choose $u$ with $p_1(u)=-p_2(v)$. Exactness of the original sequences [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence] identifies $\ker(q_1)$ with $L$ by $l\mapsto(0,c_2(l))$, and $\ker(q_2)$ with $K$ by $k\mapsto(c_1(k),0)$. Thus $0\to L\to N\xrightarrow{q_1}P_1\to0$ and $0\to K\to N\xrightarrow{q_2}P_2\to0$ are short exact.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00O3 (lemma-Schanuel), proof, first paragraph, lines 26513-26519

proof.text: Since $P_1$ and $P_2$ are projective [def-weil-pbc-projective-module], apply [lem-weil-pbc-ses-projective-quotient-splits] to the two short exact sequences of Step 1. Obtain $R$-linear sections $s_1:P_1\to N$ and $s_2:P_2\to N$ with $q_1s_1=\mathrm{id}_{P_1}$ and $q_2s_2=\mathrm{id}_{P_2}$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00O3 (lemma-Schanuel), proof, first paragraph, lines 26519-26521

proof.text: The first section gives an $R$-linear isomorphism $L\oplus P_1\to N$, $(l,u)\mapsto(0,c_2(l))+s_1(u)$. Indeed, for $n\in N$, $n-s_1(q_1(n))$ belongs to $\ker(q_1)$, so Step 1 gives a unique $l\in L$ with $n-s_1(q_1(n))=(0,c_2(l))$; this is the inverse image of $n$ together with $q_1(n)$. Similarly $K\oplus P_2\to N$, $(k,v)\mapsto(c_1(k),0)+s_2(v)$, is an $R$-linear isomorphism with inverse obtained from $n-s_2(q_2(n))\in\ker(q_2)$. Composing the second isomorphism with the inverse of the first yields $K\oplus P_2\cong L\oplus P_1$.
